inline.s: The Amitābha Sutra has two translations. One is the Buddha Speaks of Amitābha Sutra translated by Master Kumarajiva in the Later Qin period, commonly called the Qin translation; the other is the Sutra of Praising the Pure Land and the Buddha's Embrace translated by Master Xuanzang in the Tang dynasty, commonly called the Tang translation. Master Kumarajiva, responding to the Chinese preference for brevity, translated mainly by meaning, so that the text is terse and the meaning rich, exquisite and fluent. Master Xuanzang, by contrast, translated word by word, accurately and completely, striving to preserve the original.
In the Sutra of Praising the Pure Land and the Buddha's Embrace, the World-Honored One teaches:
"All you sentient beings should believe in and accept this praise of the inconceivable merits of the Buddha-land — the Dharma gate by which all
Buddhas accept and protect

Therefore, reciting the Buddha's name and seeking birth in the Pure Land is a Dharma gate by which all Buddhas accept and protect beings, and in this sutra the World-Honored One concretely and clearly teaches how to practice this Dharma gate.
After the World-Honored One spoke of

"good men or good women of pure faith who hear this name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life with its immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable merits, and the adornment of the merits of the Land of Ultimate Bliss; having heard it, they reflect on it, and for one day and night, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven, they keep their thoughts bound without confusion. When such good men or good women approach the end of life, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, together with his immeasurable assembly of śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas, surrounds them before and behind and comes to stand before them, compassionately blessing and supporting them so that their minds are not confused. Once they have cast off their lives, they follow the Buddha's assembly and are born in the pure Buddha-land, the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Immeasurable Life"
, he immediately said:
"If good men or good women of pure faith hear this name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life with its inconceivable merits, and of the pure Buddha-land of Ultimate Bliss,
they should all believe, accept, and vow, practice as taught, and be born in that Buddha-land.

Here the World-Honored One sets forth faith, vows, and practice with complete clarity: faith is "believing and accepting"; vows are "making the vow"; practice is "practicing as taught" — keeping one's thoughts bound without confusion.

When faith and vows remain only in the head, they are merely a kind of thought. Faith and vows must be put into practice; only then are they true faith and sincere vows. Therefore true faith and sincere vows necessarily lead to vigorous practice. Without real, diligent cultivation, how can one prove what one believes, or fulfill what one vows? Faith and vows without vigorous practice are no more than empty faith and shallow vows.

In this sutra the World-Honored One emphasizes again and again, repeatedly and insistently, that one must "practice as taught," and clearly tells us: if one only practices as taught, one will be accepted and protected by the Buddhas of the ten directions, will surely be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and will never retreat, swiftly realizing the fruit of Buddhahood — his concern and solicitude overflow in every word. The World-Honored One teaches:

If good men or good women of pure faith hear this name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life with its inconceivable merits, and of the pure Buddha-land of Ultimate Bliss, they should all believe, accept, and vow,
practice as taught
, and be born in that Buddha-land."
Those who practice as taught

, will all surely attain non-retrogression in anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, and will all surely be born in the pure Buddha-land, the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. Therefore, Śāriputra, all you sentient beings should
believe, accept, and understand the words of me and of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions
, and should diligently strive,
practice as taught
, and give rise to no doubt or hesitation."
Those who practice as taught

, will all surely attain non-retrogression in anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, and will all surely be born in the pure Buddha-land, the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. Therefore, Śāriputra, if there are good men or good women of pure faith, they should all, toward the pure Buddha-land, the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Immeasurable Life, have deep faith and understanding, and vow to be born there,
not giving way to laxity

In this defiled, endurable world, in the evil time of the five defilements, if there are good men or good women of pure faith who, hearing of this Dharma which all the world finds most difficult to believe, are able to give rise to faith and understanding, to accept, uphold, and expound it,
and to practice as taught

, you should know that such people are extremely rare, having planted good roots in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas. When such people reach the end of life, they will surely be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, enjoying the Mahāyāna Dharma-bliss of the pure Buddha-land adorned with every kind of merit."

Therefore, the Pure Land practitioner must with deep faith understand the meaning of "practicing as taught," and put it into action, striving day by day without slackening, pressing ever forward. The Vimalakirti Sutra says: "If you wish to obtain the pure land, purify your mind; as the mind is purified, so is the Buddha-land purified." The mind of living beings is like water, and Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When the water of the mind is clear and still, corresponding to the Pure Land (the Land of Ultimate Bliss), the moon of the Buddha appears before one; when the water of the mind is turbid and disturbed, corresponding to the defiled land (the Saha world), the moon of the Buddha does not show forth. Therefore the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation is to gather in all six sense faculties and continue pure mindfulness without interruption, so that the turbid, disturbed water of the mind is clarified (one mind undisturbed), and then to remove the mud and leave pure water (the samādhi of Buddha-recitation).

Its outline of cultivation is: true faith and earnest vows, one mind undisturbed (thoughts bound without confusion). Because of true faith, the eye of one's view of what lies ahead is clear, and one sees the goal and the path distinctly; because of earnest vows, one's driving force is incomparably powerful, surging and irresistible. Therefore, with true faith and earnest vows, one will surely follow the World-Honored One's earnest instruction to "practice as taught," and will arrive at the wondrous practice of one mind undisturbed, and by this wondrous practice will prove what one believes and fulfill what one vows.

Concerning the relationship among true faith, earnest vows, and steadfast practice, Master Chewu (the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school) teaches: "As for those without faith, let us set them aside for the moment (those who do not believe, set them aside and do not speak of them). But even among those who believe: to believe yet not vow is still not to believe. To vow yet not practice is still not to vow. To practice yet not vigorously is still not to practice. The reason practice is not vigorous is that the vow is not earnest. The reason the vow is not earnest is that the faith is not true. In short, to give rise to true faith is difficult. If faith is truly genuine, the vow will naturally be earnest. If the vow is truly earnest, the practice will naturally be vigorous. With true and earnest faith and vows, together with brave and vigorous practice, one will surely be born in the Pure Land, surely see Amitābha, surely realize the three kinds of non-retrogression, and surely in one lifetime succeed to Buddhahood." (The Collected Works of Master Chewu)

[the three kinds of non-retrogression] 1. Non-retrogression of position — not falling back from the position one has attained in cultivation; 2. Non-retrogression of practice — not falling back from the practices one has undertaken; 3. Non-retrogression of mindfulness — not turning back from right mindfulness.

The eleventh patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Xing'an, says: "Again, there are those who talk of the Pure Land with their mouths while their hearts cling to the Saha world; this too is not the vow. Moreover, the single word 'vow' includes faith and practice. Faith means that the cause and effect of self and others, of principle and phenomenon, are not false (original note: to believe that one's own mind is Buddha, and that others are the same; that reciting the Buddha's name is the cause and being born and attaining Buddhahood is the fruit; that the Western Land is phenomenon and the nature apart from the mind is principle — each one true, hence 'not false'); practice means to devote oneself solely to upholding the Name, without distraction and without scattering; vow means that the mind delights in it with every thought, and seeks it with every recollection. These three things, not one of them may be lacking. There are those who have faith and practice but no vow, but there has never been one who has the vow without faith and practice. Question: Someone hears of the Pure Land of the West and his mind delights in it, yet he does not recite the Buddha's name — can he be born there? Answer: If his mind truly delights in it, he will surely give rise to seeking; if he gives rise to seeking, he will surely recite the Buddha's name. To delight in it yet not seek it is surely not to delight in it; to seek it yet not recite the Buddha's name — how can that be seeking? One who delights in it, seeks it, and recites the Buddha's name yet is not born there — there has never been such a one. Question: There are those who delight in it, seek it, and recite, but whose worldly mind is heavy and who greedily cling to the dust and toil of the world — can they be born there? Answer: If only the general is brave, there is no fear that the bandits are strong. If the mind of seeking is earnest and the mind of recollection is concentrated, then even though the clinging is heavy, it will naturally and gradually grow light, and one will also be born there. It is like giving up silver for gold, or giving up fish for bear's paw — what difficulty is there in that? The only fear is that the power of the vow cannot withstand the power of craving, and the Buddha-recitation cannot overcome the thoughts of desire, so that one drifts along vaguely, half believing and half doubting — then I truly can do nothing for such a person." (Notes on the Essay on the Western Pure Land)
[the only fear] I only fear. [then I truly can do nothing for him] (toward such a person) I truly have no way to deal with him. "Mo" means "none."

One mind undisturbed (thoughts bound without confusion) is what Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta called "pure mindfulness in unbroken succession," and it is also what Master Shandao (the second patriarch of the Pure Land school) called "thought following thought in continuity." Master Shandao says: "Therefore the Great Sage (Śākyamuni Buddha), out of compassion and pity, directly urges us to recite the name exclusively. Precisely because reciting the name is easy, continuity brings birth. If one can keep thought following thought in continuity, taking the end of life as the term, then of ten, ten will be born; of a hundred, a hundred will be born.

May all people think well on this for themselves: in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, you must sternly discipline the mind and master yourself, not ceasing day or night. When the last thought of this life ends, the very next thought is born there, forever enjoying the unconditioned Dharma-bliss, even unto Buddhahood — is this not delightful!" (Essentials of Buddha-Recitation, "Master Shandao of the Tang on the Two Practices, Exclusive and Mixed — Abridged")

Therefore, the continuity of one's daily Buddha-recitation, thought following thought, is the guarantee of clear right mindfulness at the moment of death; and clear right mindfulness at the moment of death is in turn the key to being born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
